provenance: 24 balanced, manually authored and source-checked claim/evidence pairs based on Ada's public-only FlashAttention-3 run. Evidence is paraphrased from the paper and author blog. This narrow benchmark evaluates claim-verdict behavior, not end-to-end research quality.

sources.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision (paper)

model_verdicts.reason: Evidence states the paper describes using Tensor Core and TMA asynchrony to overlap computation and data movement, matching the claim.
Evidence explicitly mentions interleaving block-wise matrix multiplication and softmax operations, which aligns with the claim.
Evidence reports up to 740 TFLOPs/s and 75% H100 utilization for FP16 FlashAttention-3, directly supporting the claim.
Evidence says FP8 FlashAttention-3 performance is close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s, matching the claim.
Evidence indicates FlashAttention-3 speedups of 1.5x to 2.0x over FlashAttention-2 on H100 with FP16, exactly as claimed.
Evidence reports 2.6x lower numerical error for FP8 FlashAttention-3 compared to a baseline, supporting the claim.
Evidence describes FlashAttention-2 reaching 35% utilization on H100, which aligns with the claim.
Evidence lists block quantization and incoherent processing as techniques for using hardware support for low-precision FP8, confirming the claim.
Evidence supports a 1.5x‑2.0x speedup for attention on H100 with FP16 versus FlashAttention‑2, not for every Transformer workload.
Evidence shows a 2.6× lower numerical error for FP8 only; no FP16 error reduction is reported.
Evidence reports up to 75% utilization on the H100 GPU for FP16, not on all Hopper GPUs.
Evidence lists multiple techniques (asynchrony, interleaving, low‑precision), so asynchrony alone does not account for all performance gains.
Evidence indicates performance up to 740 TFLOPs/s on H100, not exactly that value for every H100 configuration.
Evidence compares FP8 to a baseline FP8 implementation, without any comparison to FP16 accuracy.
Evidence is limited to Hopper H100 results and does not establish equal speedups across all GPU architectures.
Evidence concerns attention‑level speedup versus FlashAttention‑2 on H100, not end‑to‑end LLM serving latency.

limitations: This narrow single-topic benchmark measures claim-verdict behavior, not end-to-end research quality or general-domain accuracy.
Claim-support judgments are model outputs and require human review before being treated as labels.
A missing or invalid verdict is counted as unanswered, not silently dropped.
Langfuse trace delivery is not confirmed unless langfuse_health is healthy.
